title: Fractions (Intro)
description: Class 3 IMO — Introduction to fractions: half, one-third, one-fourth, numerator and denominator, like fractions, comparing unit fractions, and adding or subtracting like fractions.

topics.title: Half, Third, Fourth & the Parts of a Fraction
topics.concept:
A fraction shows equal parts of a whole. If a chapati is cut into 2 equal parts, each part is one-half (½). Into 3 equal parts gives one-third (⅓), and into 4 equal parts gives one-fourth (¼).

In a fraction the top number is the numerator (how many parts we take) and the bottom number is the denominator (how many equal parts in all). In ¾ the numerator is 3 and the denominator is 4.

examples.problem: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. What fraction is 1 slice?
In the fraction ⅖, what is the denominator?
examples.solution: The bottom number is 5, so the denominator is 5.

recap: A fraction shows equal parts of a whole.
Numerator = parts taken (top); denominator = total equal parts (bottom).

quiz.q: What is the numerator in ⅗?
quiz.explanation: The top number of ⅗ is 3.

topics.title: Like Fractions & Comparing Unit Fractions
topics.concept:
Like fractions have the same denominator, such as ⅖ and ⅗. A unit fraction has 1 as the numerator, such as ½, ⅓ and ¼.

For unit fractions, the smaller the denominator, the larger the fraction — because the whole is split into fewer, bigger pieces. So ½ > ⅓ > ¼ > ⅕.

examples.problem: Which is bigger, ½ or ¼?
examples.solution: ½ is bigger — halves are larger pieces than fourths.

examples.problem: Are ⅖ and ⅗ like fractions?
examples.solution: Yes — they share the same denominator, 5.

recap: Like fractions have the same denominator.
For unit fractions, a smaller denominator means a bigger fraction.

quiz.explanation: Among unit fractions, ½ has the smallest denominator, so it is the largest.
⅓ and ⅔ share the denominator 3, so they are like fractions.

topics.title: Adding & Subtracting Like Fractions
topics.concept:
To add or subtract like fractions, keep the denominator the same and only add or subtract the numerators. For example, ⅖ + ⅕ = ⅗, and ¾ − ¼ = 2/4, which is the same as ½.

This works because the pieces are all the same size, so we simply count how many pieces we have.
recap: Add/subtract only the numerators; keep the denominator.

questions.q: Which unit fraction is the largest?
questions.explanation: The smaller the denominator, the larger the unit fraction, so ½ is largest.

questions.q: Which is the odd one out (three are unit fractions)?
questions.explanation: ⅔ has numerator 2; the others have numerator 1, so they are unit fractions.

questions.q: ½ of 10 = 5 and ½ of 8 = 4, so ½ of 6 = ___ ?
What is ¼ + ¼ + ¼ + ¼?
What is the numerator in ⅗?
Which fraction is bigger, ⅔ or ⅓?
questions.explanation: ⅔ is two parts and ⅓ is one part of the same whole, so ⅔ is bigger.

questions.q: A cake is cut into 4 equal pieces and Riya eats 1. What fraction did she eat?
questions.explanation: 1 out of 4 equal pieces is ¼.

questions.q: A chocolate bar has 9 equal squares. How many squares are ⅓ of the bar?
A jug is filled ¼ in the morning and ¼ more at noon. How full is it now?
Two-fifths of 20 students play cricket. How many students is that?
questions.explanation: ⅕ of 20 = 4, so ⅖ of 20 = 2 × 4 = 8 students.
